speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CANADIAN ACTION RESPECTING
speechtext:
I should like to deal with a question, as usual of national and international significance, asked by the hon. member for Kootenay West on November 15 last dealing with the policy of the government of West Germany in meeting claims arising from nazi persecution.
Since 1952, Mr. Speaker, some 7,000 Canadians have received from the German war claims fund compensation for war losses under the nazi regime, including maltreatment, amounting to almost $9 million. In conformity with the usual international practice in such matters, only persons who were Canadian citizens at the time of loss were eligible under the war claims fund, which derived from liquidated German assets.
At the same time, the West German government in the post-war period has enacted a series of indemnification laws providing compensation for victims of the nazi regime. A number of persons who became Canadian citizens after the war and who were accordingly not eligible under the Canadian war claims fund have been successful in obtaining compensation under these West German indemnification laws. Further legislative measures extending and liberalizing the scope of payments to various categories of victims of nazi persecution are currently before the West German parliament. I can assure my hon. friend that the details of these new West German compensation measures, when enacted, will be available to any Canadians who may be interested.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture why the federal government has rejected all bids to purchase 80 million pounds of stored butter oil and has returned cheques which offered 25J cents a pound for this butter oil, as reported in the Montreal Gazette of this morning.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: REPORTED REFUSAL OF OFFERS TO PURCHASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 8, 1983 the agricultural stabilization board offered butter oil for export to designated countries at 30 cents per pound. While no sales were made at this price, exporters expressed considerable interest in the product and certain counter proposals were received by the board. Because of this, the board notified all known interested parties that they should submit their best offers for the product. Firm offers with deposits were then received covering a relatively small percentage of the total amount available. In the opinion of the board these offers were not acceptable either from the standpoint of price or conditions of sale. The offers were accordingly rejected and the deposits were returned.
The board then offered the butter oil for export, once again to designated countries, at 27 cents per pound with certain provisions concerning a performance guarantee. This offer is still in effect, and the board has made sales and received commitments covering a substantial portion of the entire product.

That it is expedient to amend the National Centennial Act to change its short title from the National Centennial Act to the Centennial of Confederation Act and to change the title of the national centennial administration to that of the centennial commission; to provide also that the centennial commission shall consist of a commissioner, an associate commissioner and not more
National Centennial Act than twelve directors in lieu of eight directors and to provide further for certain administrative changes in connection therewith.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS CHANGING NAME, ENLARGING MEMBERSHIP OF ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister plan to make a statement?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS CHANGING NAME, ENLARGING MEMBERSHIP OF ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to speak at any length on the meaning and contents of the resolution before us, because I consider that it expresses very clearly what it intends to achieve.
First of all, the resolution aims at increasing the number of directors from eight to 12. In this way the government simply wants to obtain a fairer area representation and a more adequate intercommunication in a field where it is particularly important to maintain continuous relations and consultation with the various parts of this country and individual groups.
The resolution further aims at giving to the board of directors the necessary authority to undertake, or contribute to, any project without first obtaining the permission or agreement of the governor in council, as long as the required expense does not exceed the amount of $25,000. We believe that this change is desirable, because it will give the board of directors greater flexibility and efficiency.
Finally, the third objective is to amend more particularly in the French version, certain terms of the present act which are not in keeping with historical facts and to which the government of Quebec has strongly objected. For instance, both versions of the act mention the centenary of Canada rather than the centenary of confederation. Moreover, the word "national" in the English version is confusing in the context in which it is used, and resulted in another historical error in the French version. Thus, the latter constantly refers to the "centenary of the nation" rather than to the "centenary of confederation."
The expressions "Canada centennial", "cen-tenaire du Canada", "national centennial" and "centenaire de la nation" have given rise to perfectly justified objections on the part of the premier of the province of Quebec.
He set down those objections in an exchange of correspondence first with the former prime minister of Canada and then with the present Prime Minister. That correspondence began on October 4, 1961, and has already been tabled in this house by the Minister of Justice, on June 27 of this year to be exact.

National Centennial Act
That correspondence and the debates which took place last summer in the legislative assembly show quite clearly that the government of Quebec will refuse to participate in the centennial celebrations, unless the changes we are proposing today are accepted by the Canadian parliament.
Other changes less important than those are being proposed but, in my opinion, the hon. members will be in a better position to discuss them at the second reading stage of the bill.
Therefore, I do not intend to say anything more at this time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS CHANGING NAME, ENLARGING MEMBERSHIP OF ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I am somewhat surprised, Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister, in whose name this bill appears, has not spoken on this amendment but has left this matter to the President of the Privy Council. I will be speaking at somewhat greater length than he did. The President of the Privy Council has set forth, in simple words, that the reason for these changes is the high minded purpose of the government to bring about an increase in the number of officials and to increase the number of directors from 8 to 12; to improve the efficiency of liaison, as I understand it, by a provision that the governor in council will not be required to give his consent to undertakings or projects costing under $25,000; and finally to change the name because the premier of Quebec has stated that unless this change is made, that province will not cooperate in the celebration of the one hundredth year of Canada's confederation. We have heard of other ultimatums in recent months. Apparently, from the very careful wording of the President of the Privy Council, this is another of those ultimata which have become very prevalent in the course of the past seven or eight months.

Mention was made of the fact that there had been communication with me, as prime minister, by the premier of Quebec. I would point out that, while I have not the record before me, he stated that the date of that letter was October 4, 1961, and it will be noted that the act in question was assented to on September 29, 1961. In other words, throughout the entire period of the debate that went on in connection with this matter, this question was not raised by the premier of Quebec. It was only when he was asked to make recommendations in regard to the representation of Quebec on this board of directors that, as I recall it, for the first time any suggestion was made in this connection.
I do not think it is quite as simple as the President of the Privy Council would have

it. You will have noticed, sir, that the number of directors is to be increased. That is becoming something of a regular course; as soon as the number is increased, immediately any appointments to that board of directors will be of those who are considered to be politically fit. I am sure that in a matter as important as securing the co-operation of all parts of Canada, considerations of political fitness will not be the pre-eminent reason for appointments to this non-party crusade, as it were, on the part of Canadians to bring about a realization in all parts of our country of the meaning of our 100 years of confederation. I believe there is need of a strong centennial administration without regard to party.
A little later on I am going to ask the President of the Privy Council to place on record the list of appointments that have been made to the conference. It is an interesting list, and it is one to which I shall refer. It is one that in my opinion gives greater consideration to political fitness, to patronage packing, than to the great issues that face us and the opportunity of doing something in Canada to bring together all parts of this country in a unity of dedication.

Now, sir, we believe that in the appointments to be made to this council, patronage should not be put on the march, that partisan political objectives have no place in an organization designed to bring together all the people of Canada and all the provinces of Canada. I intend to look over, just in a casual way, the appointments which have already been made since the minister took charge. I am not going to say there would not be occasions when I would not raise objection, but this is something which is, or should be, above party, above any consideration other than the unity of our country.
I object strenuously to this list. It is a list which indicates that this government has no realization of the meaning of a celebration of confederation. It discloses the appointment of several people in a representative capacity but the rest of them, many of them, have no other practical qualification except that they are all members of the party which is now in power. I do not understand this in the context we are now considering. A committee which should be representative of all the people of Canada should be above the suggestion of becoming a party instrument in overwhelming measure.
Now the intention is to increase the number of directors. What does this mean? It means that all the appointments which have been made are out because as soon as the act is amended-

I want to look back and see what was decided in the past, and ask why the changes? I go back to the first meeting of the provisional national committee. I do this merely for the purpose of having the record clear. It met under the joint chairmanship of the hon. member for Three Rivers and the hon. member for Queens. That was on February 8, 1960. On this committee there is the President of the Privy Council and the Minister of Forestry. Those ministers represent something of the relationship that we endeavour to bring out. It is a joint relationship between the English and the French. We had joint representation in regard to the appointments made outside of those who were appointed by the provinces.
The minister has opened up the whole field by saying that he wants to make this a strong and effective organization. What has been done? What are we going to achieve? Are we going to attain what we hope will be a time of national stocktaking, a rededication for the future? Are we going to attain a program which will mark the birth of this nation as a


nation? That would not disregard what took place prior to 1867, when we were not a nation. We were at that time a composite of colonies. There was Lower Canada and Upper Canada, and they were joined together either under the act of union or the constitutional act of 1791. But we did not have a nation. We also had colonies by the sea; Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick. They joined together as a nation on July 1, 1867. These are not my words in 1963; they were the words that Sir Georges Etienne Cartier used in 1867: "We have joined together as a nation".
Great things had been done prior to that time. In what is now known as French Canada there had been a great heritage of several hundred years. In English Canada and in the maritimes-and taking Nova Scotia, for a moment, as an example-there were the knighthoods established under James I of England and James VI of Scotland. Parliamentary institutions were established there, but there was no Canadian nation as such. There were a number of colonies which joined together following the meeting in Charlottetown and later in Quebec, and they joined together under a federal system as a nation.
I think the programs, marking as they do the birth of this nation, must have a strong national flavour. But they must also have local and provincial aspects. I see this celebration in 1967 as something which will reflect the entire record of Canadian history from the days of Jacques Cartier and the Cabots. I see it as something which will show the tremendous contribution made by the church; by the French missionaries who came here; by the French and English explorers who came here; and by those of other racial origins who came to this country prior to 1867.

speechtext:
When I hear that interruption I think of the hon. gentleman in the words of Job: "Who is this that darkeneth counsel by words without knowledge?" I am glad to see there has been special recognition of the undertaking of projects of a capital nature; that there has been recognition of the contribution made by Charlottetown, a contribution recognized in the great edifice now being built in that city. The recognition of what took place in the city of Quebec is above parties; this is a matter that should bring all of us together without regard to party, which will serve to record and preserve our historical and cultural past so as to recognize in particular the contributions made by both English and French.

I also want to underline and emphasize the contribution made by other racial origins who do not want their descendants placed in the position of being second class citizens in this confederation. These racial origins came early in what is now Nova Scotia. The Germans came in about 1758. In other parts the United Empire Loyalists came in the 1780's, many of them being of German and Dutch origin. Other races came in later on to make their contribution to the building of this country into a great nation. At the same time that recognition was given to the basic principle upon which confederation was established there was the assurance that the rights of the basic races should be retained, unchanged and unchanging.
With a view to bringing these things about we suggested certain courses to be followed. The hon. member for Three Rivers, as one of the joint chairmen, announced on October 11, 1961 the federal government's plan to provide for $100 million as its budget. Then he set out certain ideas and suggestions in connection therewith. May I detour for a moment to point out that one of those things was the authorization to the national capital commission to purchase properties on the east side of Sussex drive in Ottawa and restore the buildings thereon to their appearance at about the time of confederation. This was to be a mile of living history. Now it is the history of a mile which will never come into existence because of the stand taken by the government in their refusal to carry out a plan which had in it the nucleus of principles which would have made Ottawa a place not only vital and living in the present but also revealing something of the greatness of its past.
When we were in office we announced that the federal government intended to ask parliament to make grants available for projects in the various provinces, and that the federal contribution should not exceed one third of the agreed cost, and so on. In view of the fact that the minister has opened up the whole matter for consideration I should like to hear him place his plans before this house and the country.
I go back to 1946. At that time I suggested that one of the things that would do more to give us a knowledge of our past and an appreciation of our heritage would be a freedom train to travel across Canada carrying on it the treasures of our freedom beginning with Magna Carta and the Bill of Rights of 1689, in addition those things that made this country possible such as the Quebec Act of 1774. Here in Canada we have the heritage of being the first country within what is now the British commonwealth to secure freedom of religion. We did so 50 years before it was
National Centennial Act attained in the United Kingdom and we secured it from the United Kingdom parliament. Here the Jews received their freedom for the first time.
Ezekiel Hart was elected to the legislature of Lower Canada in 1807 and it was not until 1832 that his right to sit was fully recognized. Some of us have difficulty getting into parliament but although elected, Hart was not allowed in. But he and all other Jews were granted something for all time that was not extended to people of the Jewish faith in the United Kingdom until a quarter of a century later.
Here in Canada we abolished slavery in 1791 or 1792, before any other nation in what is now the western world. These are some of the things of our past. These are the living things that give strength and vitality to a nation. One of the most interesting debates one can read is that which took place following the introduction by William Pitt, the younger, of the amendment to the Quebec Act in 1791. That debate is worthy of a place in our history books representing as it does the beginning of the concept of independence while at the same time retaining the closest of relations with the motherland.
Then there is the Act of Union. These are things that are part and parcel of this nation. A freedom train would bring them together. I do not know whether Great Britain would allow Magna Carta to be brought over here from the British museum but certainly a prototype could be produced that would be a living embodiment of our freedom. When you read Magna Carta you find that for the first time religious freedom was established within the England of that day. It provided that Jewish people could lend money and could ask for repayment up to a period of seven years, beyond which they were not allowed to collect either principal or interest. Yet within a very few years one of the worst persecutions in all history took place in the England of that day.
The Magna Cartas of 1215 and 1217 and the various Magna Cartas that followed are the golden threads in the tapestry of our nationhood. That is why I suggest to the minister I should like to hear what is being done in this connection.
I should also like to know what the view of the government is with regard to those who today occupy the positions of commissioner, deputy commissioner and directors. I see there is to be a change made in the amendments so that the description of the offices will be "commissioner" and "associate commissioner". I state immediately that I agree with that. We discussed this at length when endeavouring to bring about this legislation. We referred to the associate as a deputy. I feel

I want to point out that when I announced the appointments in the house on January 25, 1963 the hon. member for Laurier, now Minister of Justice, gave his approval to the appointment of the commissioner and the deputy commissioner and pointed out that they were good men and had been well chosen.

This whole matter was dealt with at length on September 18, 1961, and discussed by the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, and by many other members. We felt at that time that we had brought about a plan that would be beneficial and would assure that confederation would be celebrated as it should be.


There is one other reference I wish to make and it has to do with the change of name. The name today is the "National Centennial Act" but apparently the word "national" is going to be removed. I do not understand that. Instead of being known as the National Centennial Act it is going to be called the "Centennial of Confederation Act". I like the word "national" covering the nation as a whole.

The word "dominion" has disappeared. During the days of Mr. St. Laurent it became an ugly word and was removed even from the telephone books. Now the word "national" is to be removed. I cannot understand the need of that change. This is a national undertaking. It is said it is objected to by the premier of Quebec. I am one of those who like to see confederation bringing us together in agreement, but surely we are not going to determine the course of a national undertaking on the basis of an ultimatum by any one of the premiers of the provinces. I should like to see words like "this nation" preserved. I know the minister mentioned the fact that there is not agreement in that regard in the province of Quebec.
This is the centennial of the establishment of this nation. This is not the centennial of Canada in its parts. It will be the centennial of all ten provinces of Canada. Certainly, to me, there is no opprobrious connotation in the word "national" in reference to this nation as a whole, nor was there any question of subservience in the term "dominion". I understand the viewpoint of some who say that in the translation there is a different connotation, but in the expression "national" there cannot be another connotation because the word is identical in both languages. Why remove a word that refers to all of the people of this nation, not only the two founding races but all the races of our country? I do not think words like these should be put on the proscript list.

speechtext: They are not.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS CHANGING NAME, ENLARGING MEMBERSHIP OF ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Well, there must be a reason for removing them. It is not just the action of one taken by caprice. I suggest that if this is to be a national organization, it should remain as a national organization, in its title and description. What we are trying to do by this legislation is to strengthen the bonds of our country. This is the purpose of the President of the Privy Council, and all of us. Then, why not give reconsideration to these conference members? I did not name them out of consideration for the fact that

I did not want to put them in their respective slots. I feel that even yet the minister should give reconsideration to this.
We worked on these appointments. I know how difficult it is, because as soon as you pick out an outstanding person belonging to another party, immediately someone will say, he has not supported us. This has nothing to do with the organization. I look at this document I received from the office, and it is similar to the kind of work one finds on John Macdonald's copy of the original draft of the British North America Act. That is one of the things that should be in the records of our country. He did not write anything, but he did a lot of doodling. He drew pictures of some of those who sat around the table. He would have been a caricaturist or cartoonist if he lived today, on the basis of the doodling he did at that time. This is part of our history. I make this plea to the minister on the basis of what is being done: Let us endeavour to forget partisanship. Outside of five or six representative persons on that council, a microscopic eye could not detect the qualifications for the positions they are occupying beyond those of political rightness at the moment.
I am making this appeal. We have a terrible responsibility today with the cleavages in our country, a responsibility to so act that it will not be said of us that we allowed confederation to be weakened. The achievement of confederation is a remarkable one, and the more one looks at it, the more he believes it was a miracle of statecraft. It is one of the miracles of the world. There were so many reasons why these various colonies should not have joined together, and yet they did. In 1775 the French colonists decided to stay as Canadians. They refused the solicitations that were made to them to throw in their lot with the 13 colonies. If it had not been for them, the Canada we have today would not have survived. Franklin put up a great argument. The French of that day answered this argument.
In the light of history, we could not have blamed them if they had listened to the exhortations of Franklin to grasp independence. As a matter of fact, one of the most interesting phases of history is the fact that we in Canada can join the United States any time we feel like it, without any vote on the part of the states of the United States, because under the articles provision is made for Canada entering on the same terms as the original 13 colonies, and that provision still stands.
We chose another course. Your ancestors and my ancestors did not come here for the
National Centennial Act purpose of following the attractive proposition that might have been the economic result of having joined the 13 colonies which became the United States. The leaders of the American revolution did not understand the French Canadian mind. They did not know that these people were first and foremost Canadians. Whatever our differences may be in this country, I belong to those who still contend that that spirit is as staunchly held today as it was in 1776 and 1867.
History is a great teacher. It was a monumental decision for them to make to merge in 1867 with the numerically greater number of people in Upper Canada, predominantly of British origin, and with the people of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, overwhelmingly of British origin. It was not an easy decision for them to make. There have been great roadblocks since; there have been many difficulties along the path since confederation.
The conference at Charlottetown should be read and reread, and become the knowledge of every student in our public schools, high schools and universities. We do not think enough of Canada. We always see things somewhere else. At the moment I am not criticizing our national broadcasting corporation, but I would like to see it portray something of the grandeur of our past, of our explorers and missionaries such as Radisson and Groseilliers, something of the beginnings in the maritime provinces, something of the United Empire Loyalists and what they stood for, something of those who opened up the western plains, the coureur des bois, the Northwesters, the Hudson Bay Company, something of the Selkirk settlers, and what they all endured in building a nation. Those things are no longer part of the traditions of our people. They do not see, feel or hear something of those traditions, and this is an opportunity to do that very thing.
The fathers of confederation met in Charlottetown and afterwards in Quebec. I think one of the best descriptions of their meeting in Quebec is:
-Macdonald, Galt, Tilley and Tupper, Cartier, Brown and McGee. They were there from French and English Canada. These fathers of confederation, in their dark Victorian clothes and stiff collars, might seem a less colourful assembly than the eighteenth century group in wigs and bright waistcoats that met in Philadelphia in 1787 to frame the American constitution. But the Quebec fathers also held in their hands the future of half a continent. And it was fitting they should meet in the old capital of New France, beside Cartier's great river of Canada. For here in the 72 resolutions that the conference drew up a new Canadian nation was born.
Sir, that is why I make this appeal. Give us a list of the people of this nation. Make this council worthy of our traditions. Strip

National Centennial Act this committee of those who, in the eyes and in the hearts of Canadians as a whole will not be looked on as representatives of the people as a whole, without regard to party or religious considerations. In doing that we will be doing something to strengthen confederation.
The fathers evolved confederation. Its genius was not founded on absolutes. Its genius was not in the absolute uniformity of opinion or belief. Its genius was not in the absence of differences. Its strength and its power-the fact it has carried on almost 100 years, and I hope will continue from generation to generation-was not in similarity or uniformity. It was in differences, but those . differences settled in reconciliation and a spirit of good will, understanding and cooperation.
In 1963, with all the elements that are today trying to pull this nation asunder, not saying it intentionally but having that effect, we need something of the abiding genius that characterized confederation and those who joined together. We need that once more as Canadians as we celebrate the one hundredth year of confederation. That spirit is tolerance, based on knowledge, of agreement in the larger things of life, and above all, by the determination that we as a nation put into this celebration the assurance that those differences shall not be permitted to pull asunder a nation whose future no one today, in the wildest dreams of imagination, can envisage.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: AMENDMENTS CHANGING NAME, ENLARGING MEMBERSHIP OF ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is probably a good thing that the government has found reasons for seeking to amend this legislation, because in so doing we are being given an


opportunity to take stock with respect to our plans for the celebration of the centennial of Canada's confederation, which is now less than four years away.
This is a subject which lends itself to references to our great history, such as those made by the Leader of the Opposition. It is a subject that lends itself to expressions of hope, faith and confidence about the future. I dare to hope that as a result of our stocktaking at this time, we may yet make of the celebration of our one hundredth birthday a worth-while event. However at this moment I think it has to be said with all candour that the chances of our having a worth-while celebration in 1967 are very slight. I place the blame for that on the party in power up until April of this year, and on the party now in power.
We have had many words about the celebration of our one hundredth birthday. We have had a great deal of talk about what is going to be done, but the fact is that already some of the projects which had been planned at the provincial and municipal levels have been cancelled, because people at these levels are unsure of what is going to be done nationally. Already precious time has been lost, not to mention the excursions into patronage that have marred this whole picture.
The Leader of the Opposition has referred to what was done by the government when he was prime minister. Part of what I want to say has already been alluded to in the question put to him by the President of the Privy Council, but may I put it on the record again. The act known as the National Centennial Act was given royal assent on September 29, 1961. The Progressive Conservative government had already been in power four years. Even that was pretty late, bearing in mind the warnings that had been given to the Canadian parliament years before, that we should start planning for this event. But even after that it took from September 29, 1961, until January 24, 1963, before the appointments of those to make up the national centennial administration were made. We have already had put on the record today the names of those who are the commissioner, the deputy commissioner and the eight directors.
I hold in my hand a copy of the first annual report of the national centennial administration, which was for the fiscal year 1962-63. I find from this that the board held its first meeting in Ottawa on February 18, 1963. I suggest that was already several years too late. What has the board done? I read from the report:
Until the end of the fiscal year, ending March 31, 1963, the commissioners were engaged in locating

office space, recruiting essential personnel, considering those projects which had already been approved by the government and developing a program which would guide the administration's operations in the ensuing months.
Then after a few short paragraphs-the report is all on one page-the commissioners make this statement:
They have emphasized that planning for the centennial must start now.
Mr. Chairman, if ever the words "too little and too late" apply, I suggest they apply to the attitude that the governments we have had in office have taken toward this important matter of planning our centennial in a way that would mark our history for what it is worth, and also in a way that would chart for us a second century that would be even greater than our first. One hesitates to make many references to what he himself or his immediate colleagues may have said or done about a matter through the years, but I think it is perhaps appropriate in this connection to remind the house that a long time ago some of us started saying that 1967 would soon be here; that if we were going to celebrate our 100th birthday appropriately, we should start planning for it well in advance.
Someone else may have thought of the idea first, but the first person I know to have suggested that we start planning for 1967 in an appropriate way is a distinguished citizen of the city of Ottawa, Mr. Walter B. Mann, head of the English department at Lisgar Collegiate Institute. Mr. Mann is a long time friend of mine, and I know that in 1950 he started suggesting a 17 year plan. He suggested then, and he did so publicly, that we should look forward to our centennial celebration as an event to be greeted, not just with the sound of trumpets and long speeches, but by launching programs of development to make the country one in 1967 of which we could really be proud. I may say that Mr. Mann's idea appealed very strongly to my sense of imagination, and in due course I began presenting this idea to the House of Commons. Back in 1954, nine years ago, I first placed on the order paper of the House of Commons a resolution which read in these terms:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of the establishment of a 100th anniversary committee, with provision for federal and provincial representation, for the purpose of planning the economic and social development of this country on a vast scale, including inter alia, housing and slum clearance, conservation, irrigation and power projects, improvements in transportation, highway construction, the elimination of grade crossings, the building of hospitals, assistance to municipal projects and other public works, and also for the purpose of planning ways and means to strengthen the economy of every section of this country; and that consideration should be given to the advisability of such a program being launched immediately and
National Centennial Act being pursued vigorously year by year so that on July 1, 1967, the people of Canada will be in a position to celebrate this nation's 100th birthday not only with fireworks and speeches but by the achievement of a land of health and abundance for all our people.
Mr. Chairman, I placed that resolution on the order paper in 1954 with high hopes. I am afraid now that all we are going to have in 1967 are the fireworks and the speeches. The resolution was not debated in 1954 or early 1955. Hon. members know what happens to resolutions if they are down at the bottom of the list. They are not reached. But in March, 1955, during the debate on a supply motion when the grievance raised was unemployment, I took the opportunity to spell out what in that year I suggested might be called a 12 year plan. This was 1955; 1967 was still 12 years away. I suggested that we start thinking in terms of our 100th birthday as an event that we would best celebrate, not just by having fireworks and speeches when that time came, but by developing the social and economic life of our country, by strengthening our economy, by improving our life in every way; that if we did this sort of thing, we would be in a position to have a birthday really worth celebrating. I think probably that speech of mine on March 2, 1955, was the first speech in the House of Commons which suggested that we had to plan well in advance for an event such as the 100th birthday of this country.
The next year, on the editorial page of the Ottawa Journal of March 8, 1956, there appeared a very interesting article entitled, "Looking towards confederation birthday", by that very able writer, I. Norman Smith. On previous occasions I have quoted portions of this article by Mr. Smith and I need not do so again, except to point out that here was a writer of ability, whose articles are well written and widely read, pointing out to us that if we were going to celebrate our 100th birthday adequately we had to plan for it well in advance. Mr. Smith pointed out then that Ottawa, this city, had made a botch of the celebration of its 100 years as a city the year before because it had not planned well in advance, and he hoped that Canada would profit from the mistake that Ottawa had made. I will read the last paragraph of Mr. Smith's article:
Finally, it must be planned now, and by men with a vivid sense of history and future, men unafraid to be called dreamers. Put such men at work now for even three weeks and they would come up with a blueprint of something that could easily prove the best thing that has happened to this country since confederation.
Others joined in that suggestion in speeches of one kind or another. As a matter of fact,

National Centennial Act on March 19, 1957, there was reported in the newspapers of the country a speech that Mr. St. Laurent, who was then prime minister, had made the day before at Hamilton. In this speech he took up the theme and suggested that if we were going to celebrate our country's centennial in a proper manner we would have to start planning right away.
There were these several voices. I have named, among others, Mr. Walter Mann. I have referred to my own resolution and to my own remarks on the subject. I have referred to Mr. I. Norman Smith. I have referred to the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent. Here were these voices in the early and middle fifties saying that 1967 was just around the corner and it was time we got started. Finally, on December 9, 1957, for the first time, in the light of what happens to private members' resolutions, the resolution I read a moment ago was reached for debate. It is interesting to note that as soon as I had moved it and uttered this one sentence: "Mr. Speaker, the resolution which I have the honour to present to the house speaks for itself," there were two interjections which read as follows, as will be found in Hansard of December 9, 1957, at page 2084:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: AMENDMENTS CHANGING NAME, ENLARGING MEMBERSHIP OF ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext: It certainly does.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS CHANGING NAME, ENLARGING MEMBERSHIP OF ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
We shall take it as read.
After I had made my speech urging the House of Commons, the parliament of Canada and the country generally to begin planning without delay for the celebration of our 100th birthday, the first speaker was Mr. John B. Hamilton, then the member for York West and also the parliamentary secretary to the minister of citizenship and immigration. The whole tone of his speech was that I was wasting the time of the house by bringing in such a resolution and that it was obviously nothing more than a resolution full of ideas which my party wished to see enacted. This was the kind of treatment given to my motion. It did not come to a vote; it was talked out.
It was interesting to read the press reports on the debate which took place that day and to read the headlines which the papers put on the reports. I have here a copy of the Montreal Gazette of December 10, 1957, and the headline on the Canadian Press story is: "C.C.F. Urges Bold Plan for 1967 Centennial". We often quarrel with the use of headlines but I am grateful for that headline; I think it caught the spirit of the resolution and of the speeches we made in support of it. The Toronto Globe and Mail of that morning ran the same story but gave it this headline: "P.C.'s spurn C.C.F. Plan for '67 Program". Well, I suppose that was a good headline, too, because if the one in


the Gazette caught the spirit of the resolution, the one in the Globe and Mail caught the attitude of the government toward the whole project. Thus it was that back in those days, probably because the idea came from some of us in this minority party, the major parties rejected it. It was then we lost the chance of having a celebration of the kind which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) now says we ought to have. In 1957 the Progressive Conservatives spurned the plan. Finally, however, four years later, in 1961, under the leadership of the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who was then prime minister, the legislation we are now being asked to amend was brought in. But it took another year and a half before people were appointed to carry on the work, and about all they have done so far is to look for office space, recruit personnel and make at long last, a decision that the time to start is now.
In the meantime, as far as references to this matter in the house are concerned, very few have been made to the legislation we now have before us. Most of the attention has been paid to the legislation respecting the world fair which was passed last year and, as hon. members are aware, there does seem to be a great deal of turmoil over that. But I suggest the turmoil surrounding the arrangements for the world fair points to the fact that I was more of a prophet than I realized when I expressed the hope in my resolution a decade ago that we would plan this event in such a way as to make sure that when July 1, 1967, came we might have, not just fireworks and speeches, but a land of health and abundance of which we could be justly proud.
I admit I have offered these remarks in a spirit which is something less than hopeful. I think we as a country lost our chance to have a proper 100th birthday celebration because neither the Liberals nor the Conservatives were prepared to look at this thing in the terms I. Norman Smith suggested in his article in the Ottawa Journal some years ago or in the terms of the speech which the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent made in Hamilton, or in the terms of my motion. Indeed, it might not have been considered at all if the provinces and municipalities, realizing that 1967 was coming, had not pressed Ottawa to give a lead. However, in spite of the fact that my observations have not been altogether hopeful, I do express confidence that because the subject has been raised today and because this question is out in the open and we must of necessity take stock of the situation, we will pull up our socks and begin to do something to make this

National Centennial Act
celebration a significant one. If we are to do this, it will call for the display of some of the things the Leader of the Opposition talked about, so that our people can see them -souvenirs, mementos of our history. It will call for an awareness on our part of the greatness of those who brought Canada into being and of our responsibility to bring into being a still greater Canada. All of this calls for a lot more than speeches and fireworks; it calls for the kind of social and economic planning which we proposed when we brought this matter up ten years ago and which we still say is the way to build a nation worthy of celebrating its 100th birthday.
I am grateful that the matter has been reopened today so that we have the opportunity to go into it and assess the position, and I hope the whole question of whether or not this will be done on a patronage basis will be brought out into the open. Surely this is no place for patronage. I was glad the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) replied so readily that the present members of the administration would not be removed. I was glad to hear him say that the additions mean just additions, not replacements. I hope a hard look will be taken at the larger group, the conference which is being formed, to make sure that those who are on the committee represent all the streams of life in this country. I must say that when I heard the Leader of the Opposition berating the government for its practice of patronage I wondered who was talking.

speechtext: Remembering what the hon. gentleman's party did while in power in Saskatchewan, he ought to start close to home in that regard.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: AMENDMENTS CHANGING NAME, ENLARGING MEMBERSHIP OF ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I will come back to Saskatchewan in a moment. Through the efforts of some of my friends in the Progressive Conservative party, the government tabled a couple of interesting sessional papers a short while ago. They were lists of consultants-two lists, one in use by the present Liberal government and one which had been in use by the government which went out of office in April of this year. They are both interesting but I think the old one is more interesting than the new one. Looking at this list-and it is an official document now, sessional paper No. 255, part 1-I find that on page 1 appears the following sentence:
With regard to Newfoundland, effective immediately. all matters pertaining to Newfoundland will be referred to Mr. James A. McGrath, M.P. and I think at the time of referral he should be supplied with the name and address of the individual who is our normal consultant concerned with the particular problem.
I go over into Ontario, no this is in Quebec, just across the river, and I find an interesting situation there. There the consultant for a certain constituency, the member of parliament for which happened to be a Liberal, was a civil servant. I shall not give his name, except that he was "Dear Tom". Here was a civil servant working for the government of the day, handling the patronage for a particular constituency.
Then I look at Saskatchewan and I find, very interestingly, that the constituency of Prince Albert is listed, and the name of the member of parliament for that constituency is given. We know his name, of course; he is the present Leader of the Opposition. The consultant, the person handling these patronage matters, is listed. I will not give her full name but I will say that the list says she was to be addressed as "Dear Bunny". I thought the Leader of the Opposition was happy to have a dog around the house, but apparently it was "Dear Bunny" when it came to handling the patronage in his constituency.
I hope hon. members will forgive me for this light touch, Mr. Chairman, but I think it necessary after listening to this tirade on the part of the Leader of the Opposition against the present government on the matter of patronage. It is pretty hard to tell which of the two older parties is more adept at that practice. At any rate, I do agree with the Leader of the Opposition that there is no place for it in the administration of our centennial legislation.
Let me say briefly that I can see reasons for increasing the size of the board, as posed in this legislation. I think we should view sympathetically the suggestion that certain changes be made in the title of the legislation and in one or two other places. Like the Leader of the Opposition, I like the word "national"; but if it causes offence in certain places, and we want to achieve unity, let us consider the objection sympathetically. I would go one step further and suggest to the President of the Privy Council that it might even be better-it is not merely a compromise but is better-to change the name to the Canadian centennial act. We are only at the resolution stage, and I should like to ask the President of the Privy Council or the Prime Minister to look at this suggestion. I think we could improve the legislation tremendously and would avoid the appearance that we are avoiding the word "national" if in all places we used the word "Canada" or "Canadian", thus making it clear that what we are proposing to celebrate is the centenary of the confederation of Canada.

National Centennial Act
I have just one other word to add about the turmoil there is around the use of the word "national". I do not think it hurts us to be reminded that there are those among us who think of Canada as having originally been founded by two nations; that we should take all that into consideration in our attempt today to recast confederation, conserving what we have, and going on to build a better Canada. This matter which is being drawn to our attention, makes us realize that what we have to face is the desire of those in the French speaking part of Canada for a greater measure of autonomy as a French speaking nation and a French speaking group, but not as a province.
Where I think we are in danger of going awry in today's situation is when people like Premier Bennett, and some others, translate this difficulty we are trying to sort out into a case of provincial rights. It is not a reversion to provincial rights that is wanted. We have rather two main groups to consider. We have the French speaking people for whom a greater measure of autonomy seems to be that which they most desire; and we have the English speaking people in the rest of Canada, to whom the benefits of federalism are just as precious as are the benefits of autonomy to the French speaking people. This, I suggest, does not mean that we want to turn our land into a squabble over provincial rights. We have to think of what the two main groups want. I think we can recast and rewrite our constitution so that those of us who so desire can have the benefits of federalism and those who wish can have the benefits of autonomy, up to a point at any rate, within the Canadian family.
I do not think we should be alarmed because the word "national" is brought out into the open in a debate like this. As an English speaking Canadian I like the word. It is a good word. I like this nation to which I belong. But I like the word "Canada" even better. The word "nation" might apply to any one of a hundred nations; but "Canada" is the area, the country, the heritage to which we all belong. Canada is the country we are trying to build for the future, and I think we can build a better Canada if we try to grapple sympathetically with the problem before us, as posed by this particular piece of legislation. I think we can help make for a better future, for a better second century, if we try now to make up for the mistakes we have made in the last few years, and make the celebration of our 100th anniversary what it should be. I have said, and I repeat, that I think precious time, maybe too much time, is being lost. When suggestions were made over the past decade they


were ignored. However, there are still three and a half to four years to go, and I think hon. members will realize that some things can still be done. I urge that this stocktaking session we are having be taken seriously, and that we do our best to plan for the kind of centennial which will be worthy of this great Canada to which we all belong.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed very seldom that the federal parliament has to deal with legislation such as Bill S-41 which seeks the authorization to build:
A bridge and a causeway on the St. Lawrence river-linking the shore of 94th avenue, in the city of Pointe-aux-Trembles, Montreal.

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE
speechtext:
-I feel that any bridge which crosses the St. Lawrence should belong to the federal government, to the province or even to a municipality, under an agreement with the federal government in many cases.
However, there was no need, in my opinion, to ask us to pass a bill of this nature to authorize the construction of a bridge which will give privileges to a private enterprise or even to a private individual.
I will say to the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) that the same thing was done elsewhere. Any time a person wishes to reach the shore opposite his home, he just has to build a bridge without asking the government's permission or without having to present a private bill. He just goes ahead and if the federal government ever needs that land or has to change something to the private bridge, it is not bound by a bill or by legislation passed by the house.
Mr. Speaker, I will read the preamble of Bill S-41:
Whereas Developpement Central Ville de L'lsle Inc., a company duly incorporated by letters patent issued under the companies act of the province of Quebec, has acquired title to, is the owner and has the control of most of the territory of two islands lying within the harbour of Montreal, namely, Isie Ste Therese and Isle-aux-Asperges, most of which territory is presently used as farmland:
It appears that Developpement Central Ville de L'lsle Inc. is the owner and has the control of the lands on Isle Ste. Therese and Isle-aux-Asperges.
Whereas to provide for the full development of this territory, it is necessary to subdivide it into residential-

Private Bills
It is all very well to build a bridge, but 1 object to a bill which would bind the federal government through the construction of a private bridge. It should be possible to find a way to build a private bridge without binding and tying up the federal government by passing a federal act to that effect.
-it is necessary to subdivide it into residential, commercial and industrial lots, under an elaborate town planning system.
Here again, it does not come under the jurisdiction of the federal government to decide or even consider whether the company in question should have an elaborate town planning system.
That rests with the municipal authorities and the provincial authorities, as is the case in Ontario. Here, in Ottawa, when you talk about town planning, it concerns the municipality and the province, even if the federal government may put forward a few suggestions.
And further on, in the preamble:
Whereas the construction of a bridge and causeway over the St. Lawrence river in the area would contribute to such development and create employment: Therefore Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I recognize that the construction of a bridge and a causeway over the St. Lawrence river would contribute to such development and create employment.
Now, what would be the length of this bridge, what would be its approximate cost?
Why is it that the federal government does not build a bridge which would span the St. Lawrence river and reach those islands where, no doubt, houses could be built in residential locations?
We do not object to the construction of a bridge by the federal government, but we are strongly opposed to the construction of a private bridge, with the agreement of the central government, sanctioned through a hill authorizing a company or an individual to become the owner of the bridge.
The first clause of the bill reads as follows:
Subject to the provisions of this act, Develop-pement Central Ville de l'lsle Inc. is authorized to construct, maintain and operate a bridge-*
Mr. Speaker, this should imply that the bridge might be a toll bridge under the circumstances, that the company itself would have the right to establish the toll rate.

-maintain and operate a bridge on the St. Lawrence river, linking the shore of 94th avenue, in the city of Pointe-aux-Trembles, Montreal, to the

shore of Ile-aux-Asperges, and causeway linking Ile-aux-Asperges and the shore of lie Ste Therese.
At the same time, when referring to the explanatory notes, we find this:
The sole purpose of this bill is to authorize the company to construct a bridge and a causeway over the St. Lawrence river thus making possible the development of two islands lying within the harbour of Montreal.
The lands involved are presently used for farming but the project will make it possible to develop them into residential, commercial and industrial properties.
The bill contains the usual safeguards, namely, that the governor in council must approve the plans and location; the company must observe such regulations for the security of navigation as may be prescribed by the governor in council; and the usual time limits are placed on the commencement and completion of construction.
Mr. Speaker, we, in this corner of the house, cannot give our support to a measure of such importance.
We are in favour of private enterprise, but we recognize that there is such a thing as public property which belongs to the people and, as such, must be protected. Now, when we have a means to cross over a stream from one side to the other, it seems to me that belongs to the federal government, just like the bridges between the north and south shores of the St. Lawrence, be they located at Montreal, Valleyfield, Quebec city or anywhere else. Those bridges do not belong to private individuals or private enterprise but to the government.
As a matter of fact, as I pointed out a while ago, some of those bridges were built thanks to contributions from the municipalities, the provinces and the federal government.

Provided, however, that if such approval is not obtained within three years after the passing of this act, the powers granted for the construction of the said bridge shall cease and be null and void.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the hon. member for Dollard, who is a man of ability and good will, should have tried to submit a more serious bill than the one brought forward. In fact, I sat in this house from 1946 to 1948 and never was such a bill introduced, asking to authorize a private corporation or an individual to build a bridge across the St. Lawrence river, or from one bank to an island located in the middle of the river, in order to facilitate the construction or creation, if you prefer, of projects which could be residential or industrial and probably commercial. Mr. Speaker, I sincerely believe that the points raised by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) in support of his amendment are not valid. Besides, when the hon. member for Villeneuve says he has never seen such a bill adopted, I think he overlooked a few, because in 1961 the house passed-

Private Bills

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE
speechtext: He should know that in 1961 the House of Commons passed a similar bill which contained almost the same sections as the one which is being studied today. It is a private company.

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE
speechtext:
As far as the St. Lawrence river is concerned, under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, an act of parliament is needed to allow a corporation to build a bridge over the St. Lawrence river, whether the waterway is to be crossed completely or in part.
In this case, it is intended to build a bridge not longer than 500 feet, so that the people concerned may move about on an island which they own. It is nothing more than that.
I am asked today to give the names of the members of that company. I am glad to do so: the president is Mr. Conrad Bock, the director is Mr. Robert Desy, notary, of Montreal and the secretary-treasurer is Miss Denise Cournoyer, also of Montreal.

If the hon. member for Lapointe had listened to me when I introduced the bill last week, he would know that I gave all those details. I explained at that time why it was impossible to build such a bridge without going through this procedure.

This island measures about 2,000 acres, 1,737 of which can be used. Out of those 1,737 acres, 1,480 are owned by the company. Moreover, the company has options on the other lands.
So far, the company has applied for the loans required for the construction of that bridge. Therefore the company is operating.

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE
speechtext:
Last week, the hon. members for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), I think, inquired about the merits of a private enterprise erecting a bridge over a stream like the one in question.
Generally speaking, I think the construction of bridges rests with both provincial and federal governments.
The proposed structure will be only 500 feet long and will make possible a private development. In my opinion, it should not be expected that either the federal government or the province will build a bridge for the sake of private individuals. I feel that if the company wishes to develop an island it owns, it should also make the necessary expenditures to get to that island.
Mr. Speaker, if the bill is given second reading, our hon. friends will have every

opportunity of discussing its various clauses when they are examined by a standing committee of the house.

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE
speechtext: We do want to bring up the subject again.

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very closely to the remarks of my hon. friend, the hon. member for Dollard, who surely did not put forward very strong arguments in his attempt to disprove the merits of the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Villeneuve.
I do not often agree with the views of that hon. member.
In my opinion, the hon. member for Villeneuve was too conservative this time in asking that this bill be hoisted for six months.

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
I feel that the hon. member should withdraw his insult to the hon. member for Villeneuve whom he called a Conservative.

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I made no reference to narrow-mindedness. If I had, the hon. member for Lapointe could have thought I was alluding to him. I actually said that the hon. member for Villeneuve had been too conservative in his remarks, because he should have suggested that consideration of the bill be postponed for a much longer period than six months.
In my humble opinion, there are reasons for which this amendment ought to be adopted.
While attempting to refute the reasons the hon. member for Villeneuve had given for moving the amendment, the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) tried to compare the Developpement Central Ville de l'lsle Inc., to the Three Rivers bridge corporation.
The two corporations have been set up for quite different purposes. In the first place, in 1961 the Three Rivers bridge corporation submitted a bill that it was my privilege to sponsor. The object of the bill was not to further private interests but to develop the economy of a whole region, that of the heart of Quebec.
The arguments marshalled then for the passing of that bill were very serious. They rested, first, on the solvency of the directors of the corporation and their business experience; moreover, they asked for the special powers needed, under the Navigable Waters Protection Act, to carry out a project studied many times over a period of years by engineers for the provincial government as well as for private enterprise.
Private Bills
With regard to this bill, the hon. member for Dollard may lack some information, and he might be very interested to learn that the corporation of Developpement Central de Ville de l'lsle Inc. would own approximately 1,400 acres of land on Ile-aux-Asperges as well as hold options on a large section of the rest of it.
I do not know whether the hon. member for Dollard is aware of the facts, but in my opinion, the members of the house ought to be. This corporation requesting special powers from this house today is on the verge of bankruptcy, so much so that the lots were bought four years ago from a mortmain corporation, and no capital and even no interest was paid for them; moreover, legal action was taken against the corporation several times before the superior court in Montreal.

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are discussing the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Villeneuve to the effect that second reading of this bill should be postponed for six months.
I respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member who now has the floor goes well beyond the limits allowed by the proposed amendment.

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE
speechtext: Reasons are being put forward.

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE
speechtext: I should like to have the opinion of the Chair.

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE
speechtext:
I do not know whether the hon. member for Dollard has been enlightened by the remarks I just made but I am of the opinion that they are in order because I stated at the very beginning that the hon. member for Villeneuve had submitted an amendment for a six months' hoist, and I am now giving the reasons for favourable consideration of this amendment. My remarks concern the proposed amendment and the solvency of the corporation asking the house for the privilege to build a bridge, and the interruption by the hon. member for Dollard will not divert me from the subject I intend to deal with.
On several occasions the company was sued before the superior court in Montreal, and often threatened with seizure and sale of its properties by the sheriff. This mortmain corporation whose name I shall not reveal, has paid its creditors to keep a mortgage on the properties sold. In addition, Mr. Bock, the president of the company sponsoring this bill, is insolvent as you will find out by inquiring from the St. James street branch of the Bank of Montreal where you will be told that Mr. Bock is unable to manage his business.
It might be a good thing to grant special powers to a corporation but not to insolvent individuals.

Private Bills
I believe that this would be a colossal mistake. Besides, the hon. member for Dollard could perhaps try to disprove the statement that the municipal council of Pointe-aux-Trembles, at their meeting of November 4 last, refused to approve the construction of that bridge because they were well aware, undoubtedly from the information received, of the hazards of unfair use of that bridge, because the powers that would be given the corporation would be practically unlimited and Ile-aux-Asperges would become a closed island, since it would then be left to the whim of the directors of that corporation to impose burdensome charges. Now, Ile-aux-Asperges being closed, its residents would have to suffer inconvenience beyond any limit compatible with individual freedom.
And that is not all. Supposing for a moment that this company could benefit from the passing of this bill, it would go before its creditors and say: "We now have authorization from the federal government to build a bridge". It would then borrow money, not to start the construction of the bridge but rather to pay off old mortgages which have not been reimbursed for four years and it would carry on with the construction of the bridge over a period of more than three years.
Then, the company would be forced to come back before us and ask for an extension of the same powers for another period of three years, but in the meantime, the creditors would not get more benefits, because this bill is introduced for the sole purpose of paying off the debts of that corporation.
The directors mentioned are unknown in financial circles, except for Mr. Conrad Bock who is recognized as being insolvent. Among the others, Miss Cournoyer has been mentioned, and I do not think that she ranks among the business personalities of the metropolis. As for the other director, I have forgotten his name.
In short, it is dangerous to grant to an insolvent company the means to recover funds which will be used for other purposes than those for which they would be granted.
The municipality of Pointe-aux-Trembles is justified in objecting to the construction of the bridge.

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE

subtopic: POINTE-AUX-TREMBLES BRIDGE
